reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard immunology references
clinicalPearls: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency is a group of autosomal recessive disorders in which neutrophils cannot adhere to and migrate across the vascular endothelium to reach sites of infection
The most common form, LAD-1, results from defects in the beta-2 integrin common chain (CD18), impairing firm adhesion of leucocytes
A cardinal clinical clue is delayed separation of the umbilical cord accompanied by omphalitis in the newborn period
Recurrent bacterial and fungal soft-tissue infections occur characteristically without pus formation, because neutrophils fail to enter the tissues
A persistently high blood neutrophil count (marked leucocytosis) is typical, since neutrophils remain in the circulation rather than migrating out
Severe gingivitis, periodontitis, and poor wound healing are frequent features

LAD-2 involves defective fucosylation of selectin ligands and is associated with the Bombay blood group and developmental abnormalities, while LAD-3 combines adhesion failure with a bleeding tendency due to impaired integrin activation in platelets
Management includes aggressive treatment of infections and antimicrobial prophylaxis, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offering cure in severe LAD-1
reference.pathophysiology: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency arises from defects in the adhesion cascade that normally allows leucocytes to roll along, firmly adhere to, and transmigrate across activated endothelium. In LAD-1, mutations in ITGB2 reduce or abolish the shared CD18 subunit of the beta-2 integrins, so neutrophils cannot form the firm adhesion needed to exit the bloodstream, leaving tissues undefended despite abundant circulating neutrophils. LAD-2 results from a defect in GDP-fucose transport that impairs synthesis of sialyl-Lewis X, the selectin ligand required for rolling, and also causes the rare Bombay phenotype and neurodevelopmental problems. LAD-3 stems from defective inside-out signalling (kindlin-3/FERMT3) that prevents activation of integrins on both leucocytes and platelets, combining infection susceptibility with a Glanzmann-like bleeding disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Glanzmann thrombasthenia (for the bleeding seen in LAD-3)
additionalInvestigations: Flow cytometry for CD18 and CD11 expression on neutrophils (reduced or absent in LAD-1)
Full blood count demonstrating marked neutrophil leucocytosis
Genetic testing (ITGB2 for LAD-1, SLC35C1 for LAD-2, FERMT3 for LAD-3)
Neutrophil adhesion and chemotaxis functional assays
Assessment of sialyl-Lewis X expression and blood group testing where LAD-2 is suspected
Platelet aggregation studies when LAD-3 is considered
redFlags: Delayed umbilical cord separation with omphalitis in a neonate requiring urgent evaluation
Severe soft-tissue or invasive infection without pus formation requiring prompt antimicrobial therapy
Life-threatening sepsis given the severe impairment of neutrophil migration
Live vaccines and non-irradiated blood products should be approached cautiously, especially peri-transplant
reference.prognosis: Severe LAD-1 with very low CD18 expression carries a high risk of early fatal infection unless corrected by haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, whereas moderate phenotypes with partial expression can survive longer with vigilant infection control; LAD-2 tends to have a milder infectious course dominated by developmental issues, and LAD-3 combines infection and bleeding risks.
pitfalls: Interpreting the high neutrophil count as ongoing bacterial infection rather than a diagnostic clue to impaired migration
Expecting pus and abscess formation and being falsely reassured by its absence
Missing the neonatal sign of delayed cord separation
Failing to distinguish the LAD subtypes, which differ in associated features and management
Delaying transplant referral in severe LAD-1
